claim: Astrocytes that serve as neural stem cells (NSCs) in the adult mouse subventricular zone (SVZ) express the histone methyltransferase EZH2.
source: Here we show that astrocytes that serve as neural stem cells (NSCs) in the adult mouse subventricular zone (SVZ) express the histone methyltransferase EZH2.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing EZH2 expression in SVZ astrocytes (Figure 1) and is directly stated in the abstract.

claim: EZH2 is required for neurogenesis independent of its role in SVZ NSC proliferation.
source: This Polycomb repressive factor is required for neurogenesis independent of its role in SVZ NSC proliferation, as Ink4a/Arf-deficiency in Ezh2-deleted SVZ NSCs rescues cell proliferation, but neurogenesis remains defective.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Ink4a/Arf deletion rescues proliferation but not neurogenesis in Ezh2-deleted cells (Figure 3F).

claim: Olig2 is a direct target of EZH2.
source: Olig2 is a direct target of EZH2, and repression of this bHLH transcription factor is critical for neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP analysis showing EZH2 and H3K27me3 enrichment at the Olig2 locus (Figure 3A,B, Figure 4A,B).

claim: Repression of Olig2 is critical for neuronal differentiation.
source: Olig2 is a direct target of EZH2, and repression of this bHLH transcription factor is critical for neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that Olig2 knockdown rescues neurogenesis in Ezh2-deleted cells (Figure 4H) and that ectopic Olig2 expression inhibits neurogenesis (Figure 4G).

claim: Ezh2 prevents the inappropriate activation of genes associated with non-SVZ neuronal subtypes.
source: Furthermore, Ezh2 prevents the inappropriate activation of genes associated with non-SVZ neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray and ChIP-seq analysis showing that Ezh2 deletion leads to increased expression of homeodomain transcription factors involved in development of non-OB neurons (Figure 4—figure supplements 3, 4, and 5).

claim: SVZ cells including local astroglia in the human brain express EZH2.
source: In the human brain, SVZ cells including local astroglia also express EZH2, correlating with postnatal neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from human brain sections showing EZH2 expression in SVZ astroglia and neuroblasts (Figure 5C,D).

claim: EZH2 expression in human SVZ correlates with postnatal neurogenesis.
source: In the human brain, SVZ cells including local astroglia also express EZH2, correlating with postnatal neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that EZH2 is present in the 1-week-old infant SVZ when neurogenesis is active, but absent at 18 months when neurogenesis is sparse (Figure 5C).

claim: EZH2 is an epigenetic regulator that distinguishes neurogenic SVZ astrocytes.
source: Thus, EZH2 is an epigenetic regulator that distinguishes neurogenic SVZ astrocytes, orchestrating distinct and separable aspects of adult stem cell biology, which has important implications for regenerative medicine and oncogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing EZH2 expression is restricted to neurogenic regions in the postnatal brain (Figure 1) and is required for multiple aspects of SVZ NSC function.

claim: EZH2 orchestrates distinct and separable aspects of adult stem cell biology.
source: Thus, EZH2 is an epigenetic regulator that distinguishes neurogenic SVZ astrocytes, orchestrating distinct and separable aspects of adult stem cell biology, which has important implications for regenerative medicine and oncogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing EZH2 regulates both proliferation (via Ink4a/Arf) and neuronal differentiation (via Olig2) through distinct mechanisms (Figure 3, Figure 4).

claim: EZH2 was detected in most cells of the cortex and striatum at postnatal day 7 (P7).
source: Using immunohistochemistry (IHC), we detected EZH2 in most cells of the cortex and striatum at postnatal day 7 (P7) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: By P15 and in adulthood (~P60), EZH2 was no longer detected by IHC in non-neurogenic brain regions.
source: However, by P15 and in adulthood (∼P60), EZH2 was no longer detected by IHC in non-neurogenic brain regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: EZH2 staining remained robust in SVZ and SGZ cells from P0 to adulthood.
source: In contrast, EZH2 staining remained robust in SVZ and SGZ cells from P0 to adulthood (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EZH2 is expressed in the entire SVZ neurogenic cell lineage, from GFAP+ type B1 astroglial cells to DLX2+ transit amplifying type C cells and DCX+ type A neuroblasts.
source: Co-IHC of EZH2 with markers of SVZ cell types demonstrated EZH2 expression in the entire neurogenic cell lineage, from the GFAP+ type B1 astroglial cells that serve as self-renewing SVZ NSC, to DLX2+ transit amplifying type C cells (Figure 1E), and finally to DCX+ type A neuroblasts that migrate from the SVZ through the rostral migratory stream (RMS) to the olfactory bulb (OB) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by co-immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: EZH2 co-localized with OLIG2 in a small subset of both type B1 and C cells in the SVZ.
source: Of note, EZH2 also co-localized with OLIG2 (Figure 1E), which is expressed in a small subset of both type B1 and C cells in the SVZ (Menn et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E and is referenced to a previous publication (Menn et al., 2006).

claim: DCX+ cells away from the OB core had decreased levels of EZH2.
source: Interestingly, DCX+ cells away from the OB core had decreased levels of EZH2, and NeuN+ neurons that populate the GCL were mostly EZH2-negative (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: NeuN+ neurons that populate the GCL were mostly EZH2-negative.
source: Interestingly, DCX+ cells away from the OB core had decreased levels of EZH2, and NeuN+ neurons that populate the GCL were mostly EZH2-negative (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: EZH2 is expressed in SVZ neurogenic astroglia, their immature daughter cells, and is gradually downregulated upon terminal differentiation.
source: These data indicate that EZH2 is expressed in SVZ neurogenic astroglia, their immature daughter cells, and is gradually downregulated upon terminal differentiation.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the data showing EZH2 expression throughout the neurogenic lineage with decreasing levels in differentiating cells (Figure 1).

claim: Both SVZ type B1 cells and local non-neurogenic, postmitotic ependymal cells arise from local radial glia shortly after birth.
source: Both SVZ type B1 cells and local non-neurogenic, postmitotic ependymal cells arise from local radial glia shortly after birth (Merkle et al., 2004; Spassky et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Merkle et al., 2004; Spassky et al., 2005).

claim: S100β+ ependymal cells were EZH2-negative.
source: Notably, S100β+ ependymal cells were EZH2-negative (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Almost all EZH2+ cells (>99%) in the postnatal SVZ express the cell cycle marker Ki67+.
source: In addition, while almost all EZH2+ cells (>99%) in the postnatal SVZ express the cell cycle marker Ki67+, only a small percentage (∼7%) of Ki67+ cells located away from the SVZ were EZH2+ (Figure 1E, data not shown), suggesting that EZH2 expression is not a strict consequence of cell proliferation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by co-immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Only a small percentage (~7%) of Ki67+ cells located away from the SVZ were EZH2+.
source: In addition, while almost all EZH2+ cells (>99%) in the postnatal SVZ express the cell cycle marker Ki67+, only a small percentage (∼7%) of Ki67+ cells located away from the SVZ were EZH2+ (Figure 1E, data not shown), suggesting that EZH2 expression is not a strict consequence of cell proliferation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: EZH2 expression is not a strict consequence of cell proliferation.
source: In addition, while almost all EZH2+ cells (>99%) in the postnatal SVZ express the cell cycle marker Ki67+, only a small percentage (∼7%) of Ki67+ cells located away from the SVZ were EZH2+ (Figure 1E, data not shown), suggesting that EZH2 expression is not a strict consequence of cell proliferation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that not all proliferating cells express EZH2.

claim: hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F animals were born at expected Mendelian ratios.
source: hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F animals were born at expected Mendelian ratios and did not exhibit gross morphological or behavioral defects as compared to their hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/+ or non-hGFAP-cre littermates (hereafter referred to as controls).
evidence: This claim is directly stated as an observation from the breeding experiments.

claim: hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F animals did not exhibit gross morphological or behavioral defects as compared to controls.
source: hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F animals were born at expected Mendelian ratios and did not exhibit gross morphological or behavioral defects as compared to their hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/+ or non-hGFAP-cre littermates (hereafter referred to as controls).
evidence: This claim is directly stated as an observation from phenotypic analysis.

claim: The cerebellar granule cell layer did not appear abnormal in hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice.
source: While the cerebellar granule cell layer did not appear abnormal, both the hippocampal dentate gyrus and OB had reduced cellularity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both the hippocampal dentate gyrus and OB had reduced cellularity in hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice.
source: While the cerebellar granule cell layer did not appear abnormal, both the hippocampal dentate gyrus and OB had reduced cellularity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the P21 OB of hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice, the density of DCX+ migratory neuroblasts was markedly decreased as compared to controls.
source: In the P21 OB of hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice, the density of DCX+ migratory neuroblasts was markedly decreased as compared to controls (Figure 2A), with no evidence of increased cell death as measured by cleaved Caspase 3 (Casp3) IHC (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no evidence of increased cell death in the OB of hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice as measured by cleaved Caspase 3 (Casp3) IHC.
source: In the P21 OB of hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice, the density of DCX+ migratory neuroblasts was markedly decreased as compared to controls (Figure 2A), with no evidence of increased cell death as measured by cleaved Caspase 3 (Casp3) IHC (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data (not shown).

claim: hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice had twofold fewer EdU+ NeuN+ OB neurons as compared to controls.
source: hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice had twofold fewer EdU+ NeuN+ OB neurons as compared to controls (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: There were no significant differences in the type C cell (DLX2+, DCX-negative) population in hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice.
source: This decrease was not due to a developmental defect in the SVZ, as we did not find any significant differences in the type C cell (DLX2+, DCX-negative) population nor a deficit in the type B cell (GFAP+, Nestin+) population in hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was no deficit in the type B cell (GFAP+, Nestin+) population in hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice.
source: This decrease was not due to a developmental defect in the SVZ, as we did not find any significant differences in the type C cell (DLX2+, DCX-negative) population nor a deficit in the type B cell (GFAP+, Nestin+) population in hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice had fourfold fewer DCX+ cells in the dorsal SVZ.
source: However, hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice had fourfold fewer DCX+ cells in the dorsal SVZ, which is the initiation of the RMS (Figure 2D,E), indicating that the decrease in OB neurogenesis relates to a deficit of neuroblast production from SVZ NSCs.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The decrease in OB neurogenesis in hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice relates to a deficit of neuroblast production from SVZ NSCs.
source: However, hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice had fourfold fewer DCX+ cells in the dorsal SVZ, which is the initiation of the RMS (Figure 2D,E), indicating that the decrease in OB neurogenesis relates to a deficit of neuroblast production from SVZ NSCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of decreased DCX+ cells in the dorsal SVZ.

claim: Acute deletion of Ezh2 by addition of 4OHT to cultures from UBC-CreERT2;Ezh2F/F mice resulted in a marked decrease in EZH2 and H3K27me3 staining.
source: Ezh2 was acutely deleted by the addition of 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4OHT) to cultures generated from UBC-CreERT2;Ezh2F/F mice (henceforth Ezh2 Δ/Δ), resulting in a marked decrease in EZH2 and H3K27me3 staining as compared to control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ezh2 Δ/Δ cultures resulted in > sixfold fewer Tuj1+ neurons after 7 d of differentiation.
source: Ezh2 Δ/Δ cultures resulted in > sixfold fewer Tuj1+ neurons after 7 d of differentiation (Figure 2F,G), while cell death as measured by immunocytochemistry (ICC) for Casp3 was not increased (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: Cell death as measured by immunocytochemistry (ICC) for Casp3 was not increased in Ezh2 Δ/Δ cultures.
source: Ezh2 Δ/Δ cultures resulted in > sixfold fewer Tuj1+ neurons after 7 d of differentiation (Figure 2F,G), while cell death as measured by immunocytochemistry (ICC) for Casp3 was not increased (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunocytochemistry data (not shown).

claim: The number of cells expressing the astrocyte marker GFAP was not significantly changed in Ezh2 Δ/Δ cells.
source: Furthermore, the number of cells expressing the astrocyte marker GFAP was not significantly changed in Ezh2 Δ/Δ cells, indicating that Ezh2 deletion affects neuronal but not astrocyte differentiation in vitro (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: Ezh2 deletion affects neuronal but not astrocyte differentiation in vitro.
source: Furthermore, the number of cells expressing the astrocyte marker GFAP was not significantly changed in Ezh2 Δ/Δ cells, indicating that Ezh2 deletion affects neuronal but not astrocyte differentiation in vitro (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that neuronal differentiation is reduced while astrocyte differentiation is unchanged.

claim: Control GFP cells generated discrete colonies of GFP+, Tuj1+ neurons.
source: After 7 d of differentiation, both control GFP and Ezh2Δ/Δ; GFP cells yielded similar percentages of GFAP+ colonies, consistent with our previous observation that Ezh2 deletion does not affect astrocyte differentiation. However, control GFP cells generated discrete colonies of GFP+, Tuj1+ neurons, while Ezh2Δ/Δ;GFP cells failed to generate any GFP+, Tuj1+ colonies in the presence of wild-type SVZ NSCs, indicating that the role of EZH2 in neurogenesis is likely cell-autonomous (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Ezh2Δ/Δ;GFP cells failed to generate any GFP+, Tuj1+ colonies in the presence of wild-type SVZ NSCs.
source: After 7 d of differentiation, both control GFP and Ezh2Δ/Δ; GFP cells yielded similar percentages of GFAP+ colonies, consistent with our previous observation that Ezh2 deletion does not affect astrocyte differentiation. However, control GFP cells generated discrete colonies of GFP+, Tuj1+ neurons, while Ezh2Δ/Δ;GFP cells failed to generate any GFP+, Tuj1+ colonies in the presence of wild-type SVZ NSCs, indicating that the role of EZH2 in neurogenesis is likely cell-autonomous (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The role of EZH2 in neurogenesis is likely cell-autonomous.
source: After 7 d of differentiation, both control GFP and Ezh2Δ/Δ; GFP cells yielded similar percentages of GFAP+ colonies, consistent with our previous observation that Ezh2 deletion does not affect astrocyte differentiation. However, control GFP cells generated discrete colonies of GFP+, Tuj1+ neurons, while Ezh2Δ/Δ;GFP cells failed to generate any GFP+, Tuj1+ colonies in the presence of wild-type SVZ NSCs, indicating that the role of EZH2 in neurogenesis is likely cell-autonomous (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Ezh2-deleted cells fail to generate neurons even in the presence of wild-type cells.

claim: Proliferation is regulated by EZH2 and other PcG members via repression of Ink4a/Arf in multiple adult stem cell populations.
source: In multiple adult stem cell populations, proliferation is regulated by EZH2 and other PcG members via repression of Ink4a/Arf (also known as Cdkn2a), which encodes the p16 and p19 cell cycle inhibitors (Ezhkova et al., 2009; Aoki et al., 2010; Juan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Ezhkova et al., 2009; Aoki et al., 2010; Juan et al., 2011).

claim: ChIP analysis of acutely isolated postnatal SVZ tissue revealed significant enrichment of EZH2 and H3K27me3 at the Ink4a/Arf locus.
source: Indeed, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis of acutely isolated postnatal SVZ tissue revealed significant enrichment of EZH2 and H3K27me3 at the Ink4a/Arf locus (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: BMI1 is required for SVZ NSC self-renewal.
source: PRC1 component BMI1—a downstream effector of H3K27me3 repression—is required for SVZ NSC self-renewal, and NSCs with Bmi1-deletion have increased expression of Ink4a (Molofsky et al., 2003; Bruggeman et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Molofsky et al., 2003; Bruggeman et al., 2005).

claim: NSCs with Bmi1-deletion have increased expression of Ink4a.
source: PRC1 component BMI1—a downstream effector of H3K27me3 repression—is required for SVZ NSC self-renewal, and NSCs with Bmi1-deletion have increased expression of Ink4a (Molofsky et al., 2003; Bruggeman et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Molofsky et al., 2003; Bruggeman et al., 2005).

claim: Ink4a expression was increased greater than twofold in Ezh2 Δ/Δ NSCs as compared to controls.
source: Consistent with these results, Ink4a expression was increased greater than twofold in Ezh2 Δ/Δ NSCs as compared to controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ezh2-deletion resulted in primary NSs that were significantly smaller than controls.
source: Ezh2-deletion resulted in primary NSs that were significantly smaller than those controls, suggestive of a defect in cell proliferation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of neurosphere sizes shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Secondary Ezh2 Δ/Δ NSs were much smaller than controls.
source: When primary NSs were dissociated and recultured at clonal density, these secondary Ezh2 Δ/Δ NSs were also much smaller than controls, further indicating that the proliferation of self-renewing SVZ NSCs requires Ezh2 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of neurosphere sizes shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The proliferation of self-renewing SVZ NSCs requires Ezh2.
source: When primary NSs were dissociated and recultured at clonal density, these secondary Ezh2 Δ/Δ NSs were also much smaller than controls, further indicating that the proliferation of self-renewing SVZ NSCs requires Ezh2 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Ezh2-deleted NSCs generate smaller neurospheres in both primary and secondary cultures.

claim: Ink4a/Arf-null SVZ NSCs with Ezh2-deletion generated primary and secondary NSs that were similar in size to those from Control;Ink4a/Arf−/− NSCs.
source: Ink4a/Arf-null SVZ NSCs with Ezh2-deletion (henceforth Ezh2Δ/Δ;Ink4a/Arf−/−) generated primary and secondary NSs that were similar in size than those from Control;Ink4a/Arf−/− NSCs (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of neurosphere sizes shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Ink4a/Arf-deficiency reverses the self-renewing proliferation defect of Ezh2-deleted NSCs.
source: Thus, Ink4a/Arf-deficiency reverses the self-renewing proliferation defect of Ezh2-deleted NSCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Ink4a/Arf deletion rescues neurosphere size in Ezh2-deleted cells.

claim: EZH2-mediated repression of the Ink4a/Arf locus is critical for the self-renewing proliferation of SVZ astroglia.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that EZH2-mediated repression of the Ink4a/Arf locus is critical for the self-renewing proliferation of SVZ astroglia.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data showing EZH2 targets Ink4a/Arf and that Ink4a/Arf deletion rescues proliferation defects.

claim: Ezh2 Δ/Δ cultures exhibited an approximately 40% decrease in BrdU incorporation as compared to control cultures.
source: Ezh2 Δ/Δ cultures exhibited an approximately 40% decrease in 5-bromo-2-deoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation as compared to control cultures; this decrease in proliferation was accompanied by a >6x decrease in the number of Tuj1+ cells after 7 d of differentiation (Figure 3F, left blue column).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of BrdU incorporation shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Ink4a/Arf-deficiency rescued the proliferation defect associated with Ezh2-deletion.
source: Consistent with our NS culture results, Ink4a/Arf-deficiency rescued the proliferation defect associated with Ezh2-deletion (Figure 3F, right blue column).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of BrdU incorporation shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Ink4a/Arf-deficiency did not rescue neurogenesis in Ezh2-deleted cells.
source: Unexpectedly, Ink4a/Arf-deficiency did not rescue neurogenesis, as Ezh2Δ/Δ;Ink4a/Arf−/− cultures still exhibited greater than sixfold fewer Tuj1+ cells compared to Control;Ink4a/Arf-/- cultures (Figure 3F, orange columns).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of Tuj1+ cells shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Ink4a/Arf-deficiency did not rescue OB neurogenesis in vivo in hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice.
source: Furthermore, Ink4a/Arf-deficiency did not rescue OB neurogenesis in vivo, as the density of DCX+ neuroblasts in the OB of hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F;Ink4a/Arf−/− mice was greatly reduced as compared to Control;Ink4a/Arf−/− mice (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: EZH2 has a role in SVZ neurogenesis that is distinct from its function in Ink4a/Arf repression.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that EZH2 has a role in SVZ neurogenesis that is distinct from its function in Ink4a/Arf repression.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Ink4a/Arf deletion rescues proliferation but not neurogenesis.

claim: Ezh2 LV infected cells produced >10-fold more Tuj1+ cells as compared to Control LV.
source: Ezh2 LV infected cells produced >10-fold more Tuj1+ cells as compared to Control LV (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Neuronal differentiation requires Ezh2-dependent gene repression independent of Ink4a/Arf regulation.
source: This rescue of neurogenesis by Ezh2 re-expression suggests that neuronal differentiation requires Ezh2-dependent gene repression independent of Ink4a/Arf regulation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Ezh2 re-expression rescues neurogenesis in Ink4a/Arf-null cells.

claim: The housekeeping gene Gapdh was not repressed with H3K27me3.
source: As expected, the housekeeping gene Gapdh was not repressed with H3K27me3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Hoxa2b was highly enriched with H3K27me3.
source: In contrast, Hoxa2b, a homeobox gene that is not normally expressed in neural cells, was highly enriched with this chromatin modification (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Olig2 locus was not enriched with H3K27me3 in proliferating SVZ NSCs.
source: Olig2 encodes a bHLH transcription factor that is expressed in cultured SVZ NSCs, and this locus was not enriched with H3K27me3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ChIP-seq analysis for H3K4me3 revealed peaks of enrichment at both Gapdh and Olig2, but not Hoxa2b.
source: Furthermore, ChIP-seq analysis for histone 3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), a chromatin modification associated with active transcription, revealed peaks of enrichment at both Gapdh and Olig2, but not Hoxa2b (Figure 4A), correlating with the transcriptional state of these loci.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H3K27me3 was strikingly increased at Olig2 in neuroblasts as compared to the GFAP+, Nestin+ cell population.
source: In contrast, H3K27me3 was strikingly increased at Olig2 in neuroblasts as compared to the GFAP+, Nestin+ cell population (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP-qPCR data from FACS-sorted cells shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ChIP analysis of acutely isolated SVZ cells identified EZH2 and H3K27me3 enrichment at Olig2.
source: Furthermore, ChIP analysis of acutely isolated SVZ cells identified EZH2 and H3K27me3 enrichment at Olig2 (Figure 3A,B), indicating that Olig2 is likely a direct target of EZH2 in the SVZ in vivo.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Olig2 is likely a direct target of EZH2 in the SVZ in vivo.
source: Furthermore, ChIP analysis of acutely isolated SVZ cells identified EZH2 and H3K27me3 enrichment at Olig2 (Figure 3A,B), indicating that Olig2 is likely a direct target of EZH2 in the SVZ in vivo.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of EZH2 and H3K27me3 enrichment at the Olig2 locus.

claim: After 1, 2, and 4 d of differentiation, Ezh2-deleted cultures had a greater proportion of OLIG2+ cells.
source: After 1, 2, and 4 d of differentiation, Ezh2-deleted cultures had a greater proportion of OLIG2+ cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: There were greater than twofold more BrdU+, OLIG2+ cells in the SVZ of hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, there were greater than twofold more BrdU+, OLIG2+ cells in the SVZ of hGFAP-cre;Ezh2F/F mice (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Ezh2-deletion in SVZ NSCs results in aberrant expression of OLIG2 both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Thus, Ezh2-deletion in SVZ NSCs results in aberrant expression of OLIG2 both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of increased OLIG2+ cells in both culture and in vivo experiments.

claim: When Dox was added during early differentiation (Day 0–3), the number of Tuj1+ neuroblasts after 7 d of differentiation was greatly reduced as compared to no-Dox control.
source: When we added Dox during early differentiation (Day 0–3), the number of Tuj1+ neuroblasts after 7 d of differentiation was greatly reduced as compared to no-Dox control (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: When Dox was added shortly after the onset of differentiation (Day 3–7), neurogenesis was not affected.
source: Interestingly, when Dox was added shortly after the onset of differentiation (Day 3–7), neurogenesis was not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Aberrant OLIG2 expression during early stages of differentiation inhibits neurogenesis from SVZ NSCs.
source: Thus, aberrant OLIG2 expression during early stages of differentiation inhibits neurogenesis from SVZ NSCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Olig2 induction during early but not late differentiation inhibits neurogenesis.

claim: Ezh2Δ/Δ;Ink4a/Arf−/− SVZ NSCs with Olig2-knockdown produced nearly threefold more Tuj1+ cells after 3 d of differentiation as compared to cells infected with the control vector.
source: Ezh2Δ/Δ;Ink4a/Arf−/− SVZ NSCs with Olig2-knockdown produced nearly threefold more Tuj1+ cells after 3 d of differentiation as compared to cells infected with the control vector with no significant increase of GFAP-positive cells (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: Olig2-knockdown in Control;Ink4a/Arf−/− SVZ NSCs did not increase neurogenesis.
source: Olig2-knockdown in Control;Ink4a/Arf−/− SVZ NSCs did not increase neurogenesis, suggesting that only aberrant Olig2 expression in Ezh2-deleted cells inhibits neuronal differentiation (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Only aberrant Olig2 expression in Ezh2-deleted cells inhibits neuronal differentiation.
source: Olig2-knockdown in Control;Ink4a/Arf−/− SVZ NSCs did not increase neurogenesis, suggesting that only aberrant Olig2 expression in Ezh2-deleted cells inhibits neuronal differentiation (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Olig2 knockdown only increases neurogenesis in Ezh2-deleted cells.

claim: EZH2 likely regulates other genes besides Olig2 for efficient neurogenesis.
source: Of note, Ezh2Δ/Δ;Ink4a/Arf−/− NSCs with Olig2-knockdown did not generate Tuj1+ cells with the same efficiency as Control;Ink4a/Arf−/− SVZ NSCs, indicating that EZH2 likely regulates other genes for efficient neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Olig2 knockdown only partially rescues neurogenesis in Ezh2-deleted cells.

claim: Many of the genes that exhibited Ezh2-dependent transcriptional repression encode for homeodomain transcription factors involved in the production of neuronal subtypes that are temporally and spatially distinct from OB interneurons.
source: Interestingly, many of the genes that exhibited Ezh2-dependent transcriptional repression encode for homeodomain transcription factors involved in the production of neuronal subtypes that are temporally and spatially distinct from OB interneurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by microarray and ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Six1, En2, and Isl1 are involved in the embryonic development of olfactory receptor, midbrain dopaminergic, and sensory neurons, respectively.
source: Examples include Six1, En2, and Isl1, which are involved in the embryonic development of olfactory receptor, midbrain dopaminergic, and sensory neurons, respectively (Simon et al., 2001; Ikeda et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2008); these loci were 'bivalent' for both H3K27me3 and H3K4me3, consistent with a 'poised' transcriptional state (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B), which is typical of key developmental genes in stem cell populations (Bernstein et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Simon et al., 2001; Ikeda et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2008) and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Six1, En2, and Isl1 loci were 'bivalent' for both H3K27me3 and H3K4me3, consistent with a 'poised' transcriptional state.
source: Examples include Six1, En2, and Isl1, which are involved in the embryonic development of olfactory receptor, midbrain dopaminergic, and sensory neurons, respectively (Simon et al., 2001; Ikeda et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2008); these loci were 'bivalent' for both H3K27me3 and H3K4me3, consistent with a 'poised' transcriptional state (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B), which is typical of key developmental genes in stem cell populations (Bernstein et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and a citation to Bernstein et al., 2006.

claim: SVZ NSCs require EZH2 for the repression of specific sets of genes including Olig2 for proper neuronal lineage specification.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that SVZ NSCs require EZH2 for the repression of specific sets of genes including Olig2 for proper neuronal lineage specification.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data showing EZH2 targets multiple genes involved in neuronal specification.

claim: Astrocytes isolated from the adult human SVZ can serve as NSCs in vitro.
source: Astrocytes isolated from the adult human SVZ can serve as NSCs in vitro (Sanai et al., 2004), and adult human SVZ neurogenesis has been described in vivo (Sanai et al., 2004; Quinones-Hinojosa et al., 2006; Curtis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Sanai et al., 2004).

claim: Adult human SVZ neurogenesis has been described in vivo.
source: Astrocytes isolated from the adult human SVZ can serve as NSCs in vitro (Sanai et al., 2004), and adult human SVZ neurogenesis has been described in vivo (Sanai et al., 2004; Quinones-Hinojosa et al., 2006; Curtis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Sanai et al., 2004; Quinones-Hinojosa et al., 2006; Curtis et al., 2007).

claim: The infant human SVZ has large numbers of DCX+ neuroblasts.
source: While the infant human SVZ has large numbers of DCX+ neuroblasts, this neurogenesis declines sharply during the first 18 months of life (Sanai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Sanai et al., 2011).

claim: Human SVZ neurogenesis declines sharply during the first 18 months of life.
source: While the infant human SVZ has large numbers of DCX+ neuroblasts, this neurogenesis declines sharply during the first 18 months of life (Sanai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Sanai et al., 2011).

claim: At gestational week 22, EZH2 was detected in many SVZ cells.
source: At gestational week 22, EZH2 was detected in many SVZ cells (Figure 5C) as well as cells in the developing neocortex (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the 1-week-old infant, EZH2 was prominent in the SVZ.
source: In the 1-week-old infant, EZH2 was prominent in the SVZ (Figure 5C), but sporadic in non-neurogenic regions more distant from the ventricle wall (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the 1-week old SVZ, EZH2 was detected in a subset of GFAP+ cells as well as clusters of DCX + cells.
source: In the 1-week old SVZ, EZH2 was detected in a subset of GFAP+ cells as well as clusters of DCX + cells (Figure 5D), indicating that EZH2 is expressed in cell types that correspond to cells of the neurogenic lineage.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: By 18 months of age, when SVZ neurogenesis is nearly extinct, EZH2+ cells were not observed in the SVZ.
source: However, by 18 months of age, when SVZ neurogenesis is nearly extinct (Sanai et al., 2011), EZH2+ cells were not observed in the SVZ (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C and a citation to Sanai et al., 2011.

claim: EZH2 is expressed in SVZ astrocytes and neuroblasts during the period of postnatal human neurogenesis.
source: Thus, EZH2 is expressed in SVZ astrocytes and neuroblasts during the period of postnatal human neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that EZH2 is present in the 1-week-old SVZ when neurogenesis is active.

claim: EZH2 is a distinguishing feature of SVZ astrocytes.
source: Our data indicate that EZH2 is a distinguishing feature of SVZ astrocytes and in part underlies the epigenetic basis of this unique form of astrocyte heterogeneity (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data showing EZH2 expression is restricted to neurogenic astrocytes.

claim: EZH2 underlies the epigenetic basis of astrocyte heterogeneity.
source: Our data indicate that EZH2 is a distinguishing feature of SVZ astrocytes and in part underlies the epigenetic basis of this unique form of astrocyte heterogeneity (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data showing EZH2's role in distinguishing neurogenic from non-neurogenic astrocytes.

claim: Most astrocytes do not generate neurons in the early postnatal brain.
source: While most astrocytes do not generate neurons in the early postnatal brain, SVZ astrocytes retain the ability to produce neurons and glia throughout life.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about astrocyte heterogeneity.

claim: SVZ astrocytes retain the ability to produce neurons and glia throughout life.
source: While most astrocytes do not generate neurons in the early postnatal brain, SVZ astrocytes retain the ability to produce neurons and glia throughout life.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about SVZ neurogenesis.

claim: SVZ astrocytes appear to have 'preserved' the multi-lineage developmental potential of their radial glial cell origin.
source: Thus, conceptually, SVZ astrocytes appear to have 'preserved' the multi-lineage developmental potential of their radial glial cell origin, whereas non-neurogenic astrocytes apparently 'lose' this stem cell characteristic (Gonzales-Roybal and Lim, 2013).
evidence: This claim is a conceptual interpretation supported by a citation to Gonzales-Roybal and Lim, 2013.

claim: Non-neurogenic astrocytes apparently 'lose' the stem cell characteristic of multi-lineage developmental potential.
source: Thus, conceptually, SVZ astrocytes appear to have 'preserved' the multi-lineage developmental potential of their radial glial cell origin, whereas non-neurogenic astrocytes apparently 'lose' this stem cell characteristic (Gonzales-Roybal and Lim, 2013).
evidence: This claim is a conceptual interpretation supported by a citation to Gonzales-Roybal and Lim, 2013.

claim: EZH2 is expressed in embryonic radial glia.
source: EZH2 is expressed in embryonic radial glia and is required for proper cortical neuron differentiation (Hirabayashi et al., 2009; Pereira et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Hirabayashi et al., 2009; Pereira et al., 2010).

claim: EZH2 is required for proper cortical neuron differentiation.
source: EZH2 is expressed in embryonic radial glia and is required for proper cortical neuron differentiation (Hirabayashi et al., 2009; Pereira et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Hirabayashi et al., 2009; Pereira et al., 2010).

claim: EZH2 expression was detected in early postnatal radial glia, including those that give rise to the SVZ astrocytes.
source: We detected EZH2 expression in early postnatal radial glia, including those that give rise to the SVZ astrocytes.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: BMI1 does not become restricted to neurogenic astrocytes and is instead also expressed in mature neurons and astrocytes of the adult brain.
source: Interestingly, PRC1 component BMI1—which is required for SVZ NSC self-renewal (Molofsky et al., 2003)—does not become similarly restricted to neurogenic astrocytes and is instead also expressed in mature neurons and astrocytes of the adult brain (Chatoo et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Molofsky et al., 2003; Chatoo et al., 2009).

claim: BMI1 is not a distinguishing feature of SVZ astrocytes.
source: This suggests that BMI1, while clearly required for adult neurogenesis, is not a distinguishing feature of SVZ astrocytes; instead, BMI1 may function more broadly in a variety of mature and immature neural cell types.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that BMI1 is expressed in multiple cell types.

claim: During the first 2 weeks of life, astrocytes isolated from the cortex can give rise to multipotent NS cultures.
source: During the first 2 weeks of life, astrocytes isolated from the cortex can give rise to multipotent NS cultures (Laywell et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Laywell et al., 2000).

claim: After the first 2 postnatal weeks, cortical astrocytes lose their ability to generate neurogenic cell cultures.
source: After these first 2 postnatal weeks, cortical astrocytes lose their ability to generate such neurogenic cell cultures.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is implied by the previous citation.

claim: The loss of neurogenic competence during postnatal development parallels the observation that EZH2 was no longer detected in the cortex by P15.
source: Intriguingly, this reported loss of neurogenic competence during postnatal development parallels our observation that EZH2 was no longer detected in the cortex by P15.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the correlation between EZH2 expression and neurogenic competence.

claim: Ectopic expression of EZH2 in cultured postnatal astrocytes induces the expression of Nestin and other markers of radial glia.
source: Furthermore, the ectopic expression of EZH2 in cultured postnatal astrocytes induces the expression of Nestin and other markers of radial glia (Sher et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Sher et al., 2011).

claim: In SVZ cells, Ink4a was enriched with both H3K27me3 and the EZH2 methyltransferase.
source: As has been found in other stem cell systems (Aloia et al., 2013), in SVZ cells, Ink4a was enriched with both H3K27me3 and the EZH2 methyltransferase.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3A,B and a citation to Aloia et al., 2013.

claim: Deletion of Ezh2 increased the expression of the p16 cell cycle inhibitor encoded by Ink4a.
source: Deletion of Ezh2 increased the expression of the p16 cell cycle inhibitor encoded by Ink4a.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ink4a repression in SVZ astrocytes requires EZH2 for the local H3K27me3 enrichment, and BMI1 is required for the subsequent transcriptional repression mediated by PRC1.
source: Given our current understanding of Polycomb-mediated gene repression (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011), these data suggest that Ink4a repression in SVZ astrocytes requires EZH2 for the local H3K27me3 enrichment, and that BMI1 is required for the subsequent transcriptional repression mediated by PRC1.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data and established knowledge of Polycomb function, supported by a citation to Margueron and Reinberg, 2011.

claim: OLIG2 is expressed in a subset of both type B1 and type C cells, but not in migratory neuroblasts.
source: Similar to cultured SVZ NSCs, OLIG2 is coexpressed with EZH2 in a subset of type B and C cells in vivo (Figure 1E). Migratory neuroblasts, however, do not express OLIG2 (Hack et al., 2005; Marshall et al., 2005), which suggested to us that this developmental regulator becomes repressed during neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Hack et al., 2005; Marshall et al., 2005) and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: EZH2 is critical for Olig2 repression during neurogenesis.
source: Our results demonstrate that EZH2 is critical for Olig2 repression, which we found to be a key aspect of SVZ neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data showing EZH2 targets Olig2 and that Olig2 repression is necessary for neurogenesis.

claim: EZH2 is well recognized for its role in maintaining stem cells in an undifferentiated state.
source: While EZH2 is well recognized for its role in maintaining stem cells in an undifferentiated state, the EZH2-dependent downregulation of Olig2 illustrates a critical function for EZH2 in cell lineage specification.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about EZH2 function.

claim: The EZH2-dependent downregulation of Olig2 illustrates a critical function for EZH2 in cell lineage specification.
source: While EZH2 is well recognized for its role in maintaining stem cells in an undifferentiated state, the EZH2-dependent downregulation of Olig2 illustrates a critical function for EZH2 in cell lineage specification.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data showing EZH2 regulates Olig2 during neuronal differentiation.

claim: In a subpopulation of SVZ cells, EZH2 was co-expressed with OLIG2.
source: In a subpopulation of SVZ cells, EZH2 was co-expressed with OLIG2 (Figure 1E), suggesting that while EZH2 is present in these cells, its repressive activities have not been localized to the Olig2 locus.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: While EZH2 is present in some SVZ cells, its repressive activities have not been localized to the Olig2 locus.
source: In a subpopulation of SVZ cells, EZH2 was co-expressed with OLIG2 (Figure 1E), suggesting that while EZH2 is present in these cells, its repressive activities have not been localized to the Olig2 locus.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that EZH2 and OLIG2 are co-expressed in some cells.

claim: EZH2 was also required to prevent the aberrant expression of many homeodomain-containing transcription factors.
source: In addition to repressing Olig2, EZH2 was also required to prevent the aberrant expression of many homeodomain-containing transcription factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, 4, and 5), including those involved in the embryonic development of non-OB neurons (Simon et al., 2001; Ikeda et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2008), suggesting that EZH2 plays a role in restricting SVZ NSCs to neuron subtypes appropriate for the OB.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by microarray and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 3, 4, and 5.

claim: EZH2 plays a role in restricting SVZ NSCs to neuron subtypes appropriate for the OB.
source: In addition to repressing Olig2, EZH2 was also required to prevent the aberrant expression of many homeodomain-containing transcription factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, 4, and 5), including those involved in the embryonic development of non-OB neurons (Simon et al., 2001; Ikeda et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2008), suggesting that EZH2 plays a role in restricting SVZ NSCs to neuron subtypes appropriate for the OB.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that EZH2 represses transcription factors involved in development of non-OB neurons.

claim: EZH2 is not observed in mature, non-neurogenic astrocytes.
source: While EZH2 was not observed in mature, non-neurogenic astrocytes, the expression of this H3K27 methyltransferase is common to high-grade gliomas, including glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) (Crea et al., 2010; Orzan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The expression of EZH2 is common to high-grade gliomas, including glioblastoma multiforme (GBM).
source: While EZH2 was not observed in mature, non-neurogenic astrocytes, the expression of this H3K27 methyltransferase is common to high-grade gliomas, including glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) (Crea et al., 2010; Orzan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Crea et al., 2010; Orzan et al., 2011).

claim: Ink4a/Arf is a tumor suppressor locus that is frequently inactivated in human GBM.
source: Given that EZH2 directly targeted Ink4a/Arf, a tumor suppressor locus that is frequently inactivated in human GBM (Brennan et al., 2013), it is possible that EZH2 in SVZ astrocytes increases their oncogenic potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Brennan et al., 2013).

claim: It is possible that EZH2 in SVZ astrocytes increases their oncogenic potential.
source: Given that EZH2 directly targeted Ink4a/Arf, a tumor suppressor locus that is frequently inactivated in human GBM (Brennan et al., 2013), it is possible that EZH2 in SVZ astrocytes increases their oncogenic potential.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the observation that EZH2 targets a tumor suppressor locus.

claim: Mouse SVZ precursors give rise to tumors more frequently than non-SVZ cells when oncogenic alterations are induced.
source: Indeed, mouse SVZ precursors give rise to tumors more frequently than non-SVZ cells when oncogenic alterations are induced (Alcantara Llaguno et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Alcantara Llaguno et al., 2009).

claim: Inhibition of EZH2 in human GBM cell lines results in decreased cell proliferation.
source: Inhibition of EZH2 in human GBM cell lines results in decreased cell proliferation (Suva et al., 2009), and in other GBMs, EZH2 knockdown results in derepression of BMPRIB, which may reduce tumorigenicity (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Suva et al., 2009).

claim: In some GBMs, EZH2 knockdown results in derepression of BMPRIB, which may reduce tumorigenicity.
source: Inhibition of EZH2 in human GBM cell lines results in decreased cell proliferation (Suva et al., 2009), and in other GBMs, EZH2 knockdown results in derepression of BMPRIB, which may reduce tumorigenicity (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Lee et al., 2008).

claim: Expression of H3.3 with a K27M mutation results in a dominant-negative inhibition of PRC2 function, leading to a global decrease in H3K27me3.
source: Expression of H3.3 with a K27M mutation results in a dominant-negative inhibition of PRC2 function, leading to a global decrease in H3K27me3, and this K27M H3.3 mutation is a major driver of pediatric high-grade glioma (Bender et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Bender et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013).

claim: The K27M H3.3 mutation is a major driver of pediatric high-grade glioma.
source: Expression of H3.3 with a K27M mutation results in a dominant-negative inhibition of PRC2 function, leading to a global decrease in H3K27me3, and this K27M H3.3 mutation is a major driver of pediatric high-grade glioma (Bender et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Bender et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013).

claim: In some gliomas, inhibition of EZH2 may reduce cell proliferation, possibly by de-repressing Ink4a/Arf.
source: In some gliomas, inhibition of EZH2 may reduce cell proliferation, possibly by de-repressing Ink4a/Arf.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the known role of EZH2 in repressing Ink4a/Arf.

claim: OLIG2 is one of most highly expressed genes in the K27M glioma subtype.
source: Intriguingly, OLIG2 is one of most highly expressed genes in the K27M glioma subtype (Chan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Chan et al., 2013).

claim: The development of EZH2 inhibitors for cancer chemotherapy will benefit from a continued understanding of the multiple, distinct roles that EZH2 plays in development and cell differentiation.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the development of EZH2 inhibitors for cancer chemotherapy will benefit from a continued understanding of the multiple, distinct roles that EZH2 plays in development and cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the combined findings about EZH2's multiple roles.

claim: Most neurogenesis in the human brain is complete by the time of birth.
source: While most neurogenesis in the human brain is complete by the time of birth, the infant brain SVZ contains many young migrating neurons (Sanai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation to Sanai et al., 2011.

claim: In the one-week old human brain, EZH2 expression was primarily observed in DCX+ neuroblasts and a subset of GFAP+ astroglia.
source: In the one-week old human brain, EZH2 expression was primarily observed in DCX+ neuroblasts and a subset of GFAP+ astroglia.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: EZH2 is expressed in GFAP+ astroglia in the human SVZ when neurogenesis is observed.
source: Thus, EZH2 is expressed in GFAP+ astroglia in the human SVZ when neurogenesis is observed.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of EZH2 in GFAP+ cells in the 1-week-old SVZ.

claim: GFAP+, EZH2+ cells were not observed in the 18-month-old human SVZ.
source: In the 18-month-old brain, when SVZ neurogenesis is sparse, we did not find EZH2+ cells in the SVZ. In particular, we did not observe GFAP+, EZH2+ cells at this time point, though we cannot rule out the existence of EZH2+ cells in other parts of the SVZ.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For the lateral ventricle SVZ region examined, the near absence of postnatal neurogenesis correlated with the loss of astroglia expressing EZH2.
source: Nevertheless, for this region of the lateral ventricle SVZ, the near absence of postnatal neurogenesis correlated with the loss of astroglia expressing EZH2.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the correlation between EZH2 expression and neurogenesis in human SVZ.

claim: The neurogenic astrocyte population in the human SVZ is transient.
source: This suggests that this specialized, neurogenic astrocyte population is transient in the human brain.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that EZH2+ astroglia are present early but absent later in development.
